desc:
Start with an array of distinct integers sorted in ascending order. Repeat this step k times: remove the last element and insert it at the front. The result is the array nums.

Given nums, return the number of steps k with 0 ≤ k < nums.length (doing nums.length steps would give the original array back, so that case is never needed). For example, starting from [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] two steps give [4, 5, 1, 2, 3], so for that input the answer is 2. A sorted array has answer 0.

Do it in O(log n) time.
constraints: nums is a sorted array after some number of the described steps
hints: Look at where the smallest element of the original sorted array ended up. What does its position say about the number of steps?
Each step pushes the smallest element one place to the right, so after k steps it sits at index k. The answer is simply the index of the minimum.
Binary search for the minimum: compare nums[mid] with nums[hi]. If it is larger, the minimum is strictly to the right of mid; otherwise it is at mid or to its left.
editorial: The smallest element starts at index 0. Every step moves each element one place to the right (the last one wraps to the front), so after k steps the smallest element is at index k. Therefore the number of steps equals the index of the minimum, and for a sorted array that index is 0.

To find that index in O(log n), keep a window [lo, hi] that always contains the minimum. Let mid be the middle. If nums[mid] > nums[hi] then the drop from large to small values happens somewhere to the right of mid, so set lo = mid + 1. Otherwise mid and everything up to hi are in increasing order, so the minimum is at mid or before it: set hi = mid. When lo == hi that index is the answer. Distinct values guarantee the comparison is never a tie. Time O(log n), space O(1).
